ety.text: Inherited from Middle English bagge, from Old Norse baggi (“bag, pack, satchel, bundle”) (whence also Old French bague (“bundle, package, sack”)); related to Old Norse bǫggr (“harm, shame; load, burden”), of uncertain origin.

senses.d: A soft container made out of cloth, paper, thin plastic, etc. and open at the top, used to hold food, commodities, and other goods.

A container made of leather, plastic, or other material, usually with a handle or handles, in which you carry personal items, or clothes or other things that you need for travelling. Includes shopping bags, schoolbags, suitcases, briefcases, handbags, backpacks, etc.
One's preference.
ex: Acid House is not my bag: I prefer the more traditional styles of music.
And from then on, his bag was silence. Silence and killing.

senses.d: An ugly woman.
The cloth-covered pillow used for first, second, and third base.
ex: The grounder hit the bag and bounced over the fielder’s head.

senses.d: First, second, or third base.
ex: He headed back to the bag.

senses.d: A breathalyzer, so named because it formerly had a plastic bag over the end to measure a set amount of breath.
A collection of objects, disregarding order, but (unlike a set) in which elements may be repeated.
A sac in animal bodies, containing some fluid or other substance.
ex: the bag of poison in the mouth of some serpents

senses.d: An udder, especially the pendulous one of a dairy cow.
ex: Meronym: teats
Her bag is coming in nicely now.

senses.d: To put into a bag.
To catch or kill, especially when fishing or hunting.
ex: We bagged three deer yesterday.
He was a fine specimen, very large and with a beautiful coat, and I wish I had had the luck to bag him.

senses.d: To gain possession of something, or to make first claim on something.
ex: the two opposition groups have bagged almost 300 of the 500 seats contested in the election.

senses.d: To steal.
To take a woman away with one as a romantic or sexual interest.
ex: When we hit the club to go and hell-raise / Probably end up baggin' the cocktail waitress

senses.d: To arrest.
ex: Free bro, free bro, we got bagged for a M

senses.d: To furnish or load with a bag.
ex: a bee bagged with his honeyed venom

senses.d: To provide with artificial ventilation via a bag valve mask (BVM) resuscitator.
To fit with a bag to collect urine.
ex: The patient was bagged for a urine analysis and stat electrolytes were drawn.

senses.d: To (cause to) swell or hang down like a full bag.
ex: The skin bags from containing morbid matter.
The brisk wind bagged the sails.

ety.text: From Middle English bagage, from Old French bagage, baguage, from bague (“bundle, sack”), of Germanic/North Germanic origin, probably from the same ultimate source as Old Norse baggi (“pack, bundle”). Compare also bag. By surface analysis, bag + -age. The old meaning of "nasty woman" likely derives from the sense of "something awkward to be carried" (compare faggot).

senses.d: Portable cases, large bags, and similar equipment for manually carrying, pushing, or pulling personal items while traveling
ex: Please put your baggage in the trunk.
Uncountable synonyms: luggage; gear; stuff

senses.d: Factors, especially psychological ones, which interfere with a person's ability to function effectively.
ex: This person has got a lot of emotional baggage.

senses.d: A woman. A female, especially one who is saucy, impudent.
ex: Shall we ask this baggage to sit down or shall we just throw her out of the window?
Betty and Molly (they were soft-hearted baggages) felt for their master--pitied their poor master!

senses.d: An army's portable equipment; its baggage train.
